item.title: Beyond mining tunnels: China's coal-rich province accelerates smarter, greener energy transition
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
This photo taken on Sept. 4, 2026 shows a view outside the main venue of the 2026 Taiyuan Energy Low-Carbon Development Forum in Taiyuan, north China's Shanxi Province. (Xinhua/Yang Chenguang)
TAIYUAN, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- From intelligent coal mines to digital power-grid management, north China's Shanxi Province is accelerating its energy transition and maintaining stable coal supplies.
As one of China's major coal-producing provinces and a key national energy base, Shanxi is seeking to make its energy system smarter, more diversified and more efficient.
The province is upgrading its traditional coal industry through smarter technologies and cleaner production, while expanding wind and solar power to diversify its energy mix. Backed by increasingly flexible power management, these efforts are reshaping how Shanxi produces, supplies and uses energy as China pursues greener development.
AUTOMATED COAL MINING
For 50-year-old Zhao Huacheng, deputy head of a fully mechanized mining team at Huayang New Material Technology Group Co., Ltd., a major coal mining enterprise in Shanxi, the transformation of coal mining is evident in his daily work.
Zhao has worked in the industry for nearly 30 years, taking on almost every frontline role in his team, from coal miner and powered-support operator to safety officer.
Huayang's No. 1 Mine, with an annual production capacity of 8.5 million tonnes, is among China's first batch of intelligent demonstration coal mines. Its intelligent mining faces use 5G technology and automated equipment to enable remote control and reduce the need for underground workers.
The number of workers required underground for a shift at Zhao's team has already fallen from 24 to 16.
Operating a coal-cutting machine was once one of the toughest jobs. Three operators had to work together, with one controlling the machine from a platform and the other two observing the terrain from the front and rear.
When the machine started up, clouds of coal dust often made it nearly impossible to see, and flying chunks of coal posed a real risk of injury. Zhao still has a scar near his right eye as a reminder.
"With advances in technology, the operator in the middle is no longer needed. The operators in front and behind can control the machine remotely from six meters away, reducing the risks," Zhao said. "We used to get bumped and bruised almost constantly. Now, such incidents are rare."
Today, intelligent equipment has taken over most labor-intensive tasks. Clean mine tunnels, dust-suppression systems and enclosed control rooms have replaced the once dusty and hazardous working conditions.
Productivity has also seen a sharp increase. A production shift that once yielded about 3,000 to 4,000 tonnes of coal can now produce 5,000 to 6,000 tonnes, according to Zhao.
The transformation at Zhao's workplace is part of a broader push to make coal mining smarter and cleaner in Shanxi. By the end of November 2025, the province had built 369 intelligent coal mines, accounting for more than one-third of the national total, as well as 75 demonstration mines for green mining.
On the national level, China aims to make virtually all types of coal mines intelligent by 2035 by leveraging advanced technologies, according to the National Development and Reform Commission.
DIVERSIFIED ENERGY SUPPLY
While making coal production smarter and cleaner, Shanxi is also reshaping its energy mix, with renewable energy becoming an increasingly important source of new capacity and power generation.
At Shanxi Jinnan Steel Group Co., Ltd. in Quwo County, Linfen City, photovoltaic panels cover unused spaces ranging from rooftops and south-facing walls to hillside slopes and areas near an artificial lake.
The company produces nearly 6 million tonnes of steel annually. Over the past five years, it has invested heavily in clean energy projects to reduce the carbon intensity of its energy consumption.
Three months ago, the company partnered with PowerChina New Energy Group Co., Ltd. to develop green electricity by tapping the region's mountainous and valley resources. The two sides plan to use a "green electricity direct supply" model to better match the company's energy needs.
"We have developed photovoltaic projects with a combined capacity of 550 megawatts, generating more than 1 billion kWh of electricity annually," said Zhang Tianfu, president of Shanxi Jinnan Steel Group Co., Ltd.
Green electricity currently accounts for 15 percent of the company's power consumption. Zhang said the company will continue expanding its renewable energy portfolio and plans to raise the share to 50 percent by 2029.
The company's growing investment in green electricity comes as renewable energy has become the main source of newly added power generation capacity and electricity generation in Shanxi.
By the end of June this year, the province's installed capacity of wind and solar power had exceeded 80 million kW. In 2020, roughly one in every seven kWh generated in Shanxi came from renewable sources. Today, despite a substantial increase in total power generation, the share has risen to one in every four kWh.
A historic shift has taken place in Shanxi's energy mix. By the end of September last year, installed capacity of new and clean energy sources accounted for 54.55 percent of the province's total, marking a historic shift from a fossil-fuel-dominated energy mix toward one led by clean energy.
SMARTER POWER MANAGEMENT
As wind and solar power generation expands, Shanxi faces a new challenge: how to accommodate increasingly variable renewable generation while keeping the power grid stable.
Virtual power plants are emerging as one solution.
Shanxi Fengxingcekong Co., Ltd. operates China's first virtual power plant participating in the electricity spot market. Nan Dou, deputy general manager of the company, said the spot market generates a new electricity price every five minutes.
The virtual power plant aggregates scattered electricity-consuming resources and dispatches them through a digital platform, using algorithms to adjust the power loads of participating enterprises in response to changes in electricity prices and grid demand.
"When electricity prices are low and renewable power generation is high, we encourage enterprises to consume more electricity, maximizing the use of renewable power. When prices are high and the grid is under pressure, we organize enterprises to reduce their loads during peak periods, helping ensure safe and stable grid operation," Nan said.
"This benefits all three sides by ensuring power supplies, facilitating renewable power consumption and reducing energy costs for enterprises," he added.
From August 2023 to June 2026, the virtual power plant helped facilitate the consumption of 350 million kWh of renewable electricity, equivalent to reducing carbon dioxide emissions by about 350,000 tonnes, the operators said. It also saved about 210 million kWh of electricity.
Over the three years since entering the electricity market, the company's ability to aggregate and dispatch resources has continued to improve. The number of users on its platform has risen from five to more than 60, while its aggregated capacity has jumped from 80,000 kW to 2.282 million kW.
"The most important improvement is that our control success rate has risen from 33 percent to 80 percent. Only by improving the quality of regulation can we achieve the desired results," Nan said.
As of September 2026, 14 virtual power plants in Shanxi had participated in market trading, aggregating 1,459 users. Their combined capacity in the Shanxi electricity market had reached 6.4548 million kW, with a maximum adjustable load of 1.545 million kW.
Traditional coal-fired power plants are also undergoing flexibility upgrades in response to market signals. The upgrades allow them to reduce output when wind and solar generation is abundant, creating more room for renewable power, and quickly ramp up output when renewable generation falls short, helping ensure electricity supplies.
More than half of Shanxi's coal-fired power generating units have completed such flexibility upgrades.
"Guided by market needs, Shanxi's renewable electricity utilization rate has remained above 90 percent," said Zhang Chao, an official in charge of the spot market at the Dispatching and Control Center of State Grid Shanxi Electric Power Co., Ltd.

item.title: China's railway passenger trips hit record single-day high
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
Passengers line up at the boarding gates at Shenzhen North Railway Station in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, October 1, 2026. /VCG
China's railway network handled 25.204 million passenger trips on October 1, the first day of the week-long National Day holiday, setting a new single-day record, China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway) said Friday.
On October 2, the railway network is expected to handle 20.39 million passenger trips, with 1,462 additional trains scheduled to meet the high demand, the company said.
Passenger ticket pre-sales show that the most popular departure cities on Friday include Beijing, Guangzhou, Shanghai, Chengdu, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Wuhan, Xi'an, Zhengzhou and Nanjing, while popular arrival cities include Beijing, Guangzhou, Chengdu, Hangzhou, Shanghai, Wuhan, Xi'an, Zhengzhou, Nanjing and Changsha.
Routes such as Xi'an-Chengdu round trips, as well as those from Beijing to Shenyang, Zhengzhou and Qingdao are among the busiest.
Railway authorities across the country have strengthened transport organization and implemented measures to ensure safe, convenient and comfortable travel.
China Railway Taiyuan Group has coordinated with local transport departments and scenic spots to add shuttle buses linking Datong South Station with the Yungang Grottoes, a UNESCO World Heritage site featuring more than 50,000 Buddhist stone sculptures, and the Hengshan Mountain scenic area in north China's Shanxi Province.
China Railway Hohhot Group has added 11 multiple-unit trains to the Baotou-Wuhai section of the Baotou-Yinchuan high-speed railway.
China Railway Wuhan Group, tapping the newly opened Yichang-Xingshan high-speed railway, has launched a promotion campaign with local governments in Yichang and Xingshan, offering passengers exclusive discounts at scenic spots, hotels and homestays when they present their train tickets.
China Railway expects some 284 million passenger trips during the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday period, which runs from September 23 to October 8.

item.title: Extended breaks, richer experiences add momentum to China's holiday travel boom
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
Tourists interact with actors at Yangliuqing ancient town in Tianjin, north China, Oct. 3, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Ran)
BEIJING, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- China's National Day travel market kicked off on a strong note, as many travelers linked the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day breaks with their annual leave. This trend has led to longer trips and a surge in bookings for long-haul journeys, multi-city itineraries and experience-based travel products.
LONGER BREAKS, FARTHER JOURNEYS
With the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day separated by only three working days this year, some travelers used three days of leave to link the two breaks into a 13-day holiday. Trip.com Group data showed that one in every 10 travelers combined the two holidays into an extended break.
Cao Shuai, CEO of Tongcheng Travel's destination business division, said strong demand for the 13-day break has lengthened the overall consumption cycle and helped release demand for long-haul and in-depth travel.
Data from online travel platform Qunar showed that by Oct. 1, the first day of the National Day holiday, 20 percent of travelers had already reached the second city on their itineraries. Nearly 30 percent had booked hotels in at least two cities, while bookings involving stays in four or more cities surged 53 percent year on year.
For Yuan You, who works for an internet company, the 13-day break made it possible to split one holiday into two distinct stages. She planned to first spend three days in Jiuzhaigou, a UNESCO-listed scenic area in southwest China's Sichuan Province known for its turquoise lakes and waterfalls, before continuing to Chengdu for the remainder of the break.
"With such a long break, spending the whole time either resting or sightseeing can become monotonous, so I opted for a mix of both," Yuan said. In Chengdu, she chose to spend part of that extra time learning woodworking.
Longer breaks are encouraging people to travel farther. Flight bookings for journeys of more than 2,000 km rose 76 percent year on year during the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day period, accounting for more than a quarter of all flight bookings, according to Meituan.
Wang Peng, an associate researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, said the extended break has encouraged more people to start traveling earlier, spreading trips over a longer period rather than concentrating them within a few peak days. That, Wang said, could help sustain demand across tourism, accommodation and catering services for longer periods of time.

item.title: China welcomes Putin's attendance at APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, says Foreign Ministry
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
APEC China 2026-themed decorations are seen on the central green belt of a street in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, September 22, 2026. /VCG
China welcomes Russian President Vladimir Putin's attendance at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen this November, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Saturday.
Guo was responding to a question about whether the Chinese and Russian leaders would meet on the sidelines, after Russian media reported that Putin expected the meeting to yield positive results.
"The strategic guidance of head-of-state diplomacy is the most important political guarantee for the steady and sustained development of China-Russia relations," Guo said.
He added that China is ready to work with Russia to deliver fruitful outcomes for the APEC China Year.

item.title: 'China Haul' trend highlights China's growing global appeal
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
International tourists browse a Mid-Autumn Festival market at Suoxi Culture and Tourism Park in Zhangjiajie, Hunan Province, central China, September 23, 2026. /VCG
In China, where can you get the best deals on electronics and where can you find clothes that are unique, well-made and affordable?
Those are among the questions answered in a recent shopping guide by YouTube creators Kinjal and Sushi, who have 479,000 subscribers on the platform.
Pointing their cameras at Shenzhen, the couple took viewers on a shopping tour of the city, walking them through where to look for electronics, fashion and other products. Their verdict was clear: China is a "shopper’s paradise."
The video has since attracted 194,000 views, offering a glimpse into a growing trend on overseas social media: international visitors are not only coming to China to see the sights, but increasingly to shop, explore Chinese brands and share their finds online.
That trend has given rise to a new buzzword – "China Haul," with foreign visitors filming unboxing videos and showcasing what they picked up during their trips to China.
From China-made to China-bought
During this year's Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holidays, major ports across China saw a surge in inbound and outbound passenger traffic.
According to the Beijing Municipal Culture and Tourism Bureau, Beijing received 8.783 million tourist visits during the Mid-Autumn Festival holiday, generating 11.54 billion yuan ($1.72 billion) in tourism spending. Of these, 83,000 were inbound tourist visits, contributing 780 million yuan ($116 million) in spending.
At an electronics store in Kunshan, east China's Jiangsu Province, American music agent James Yin opened his backpack and showed the reporter a drone, a handheld gimbal and a wireless microphone he had picked up in China.
From drones, action cameras and other digital products to goji berry drinks and moxibustion boxes, as well as trendy toys, silk products and customized souvenirs, a growing range of Chinese goods are making their way into the luggage of foreign tourists.
A foreign visitor walks past signage in the Huaqiangbei electronics district market, Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, south China, September 3, 2026. /VCG
One widely shared comment under the "China Haul" hashtag sums up the experience: "Bring an empty suitcase when you travel to China, because you’ll shop until you’re exhausted."
The growing popularity of Chinese products reflects rising recognition among consumers overseas.
At the same time, efforts to improve the shopping experience are making it easier for international visitors to spend in China.
Shanghai, for example, has introduced seven measures to make mobile payments more convenient for international visitors, addressing payment challenges in key consumption scenarios. Efforts have also been made to streamline tax refund services for departing travelers and improve multilingual signs and visitor information in public spaces.
These measures are helping create a more international-friendly shopping environment, making it easier for overseas visitors to experience and consume Chinese products during their trips.
A two-way flow between China and the world
The growing movement of people between China and the rest of the world is creating more opportunities for cultural exchange, travel and consumption. As more international visitors come to China to explore, shop and experience everyday life, Chinese tourists are also venturing farther afield, creating a dynamic flow of people, products and experiences.
During the 2026 National Day holiday, a topic about Chinese tourists enjoying their Golden Week holiday went viral on overseas social media. Chinese travelers were spotted everywhere from crowded beaches in Australia to packed trains in Italy and popular restaurants in the UK.
Data from third-party platforms show that Chinese tourists traveled to more than 3,800 cities around the world during the holiday period, with more than 1.21 million outbound flight tickets booked, up about 4% year on year.
The surge in outbound travel has been fueled by factors including rising household purchasing power, improvements to the paid-leave system and the growing practice of combining public holidays with annual leave.
In 2025, China recorded 148 million outbound tourist trips, up 20.8% year on year, while inbound tourism reached 154 million trips, according to China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism.
The growth in both inbound and outbound travel highlights China’s role as both a major source of international tourists and a major destination, while offering a glimpse of the increasingly close interaction between China and the rest of the world.

item.title: A taste of home in orbit: How China keeps its astronauts well-fed
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
This image captured at Beijing Aerospace Control Center on May 25, 2026 shows a group picture of the crew of Shenzhou-21 and Shenzhou-23 spaceships. (Xinhua/Jin Liwang)
BEIJING, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Although called Tiangong, or "Heavenly Palace," China's space station is becoming less distant and more like home, as astronauts bring the comforting tastes into orbit.
The Chinese space kitchen now serves nearly 200 food items. Alongside dumplings and mooncakes, home-style dishes such as Kung Pao chicken, mapo tofu and fried rice have made it onto the station's menu.
Videos showing astronauts savoring freshly cooked meat and cakes in orbit have gone viral. Their smiling faces and bright eyes make the aroma almost leap off the screen.
Yang Liwei, the country's first astronaut, joked at a recent press conference that he was envious. He said astronauts can now use air-frying equipment in space and enjoy baked chicken wings in orbit. During his Shenzhou-5 mission in 2003, which lasted less than one day, his diet was limited to packaged instant food that could not be heated.
Microgravity, cosmic radiation and the enclosed cabin environment impose strict requirements on space diets. Floating particles and droplets may drift into instruments and trigger malfunctions. Since Yuri Gagarin, the first human to travel into space, paste-like food and compressed energy bars had long served as the standard meals for astronauts.
In June 2013, Wang Yaping, together with two fellow male crewmates, carried out the 15-day Shenzhou-10 space mission. People remembered this female astronaut with a ponytail for her space lecture. At the same time, the image of her floating a "zongzi," a leaf-wrapped rice dumpling, by hand also left a deep impression on the public.
Zongzi is traditionally enjoyed during the Dragon Boat Festival, which happened to coincide with the Shenzhou-10 mission that year. To help the astronauts celebrate, this special snack was added to the spaceship pantry.
Students watch Wang Yaping (R) demonstrating drinking water in China's space station, at the China Science and Technology Museum in Beijing, capital of China, Dec. 9, 2021. (Xinhua/Jin Liwang)
Eight years later, Wang spent Spring Festival aboard the Tiangong space station during the Shenzhou-13 mission. It is also China's first six-month-long space stay. Scientists customized the cuisine: for instance, they prepared dumplings with seafood fillings because Wang grew up by the sea, and plenty of spicy food for crew member Ye Guangfu, who was born in chili-obsessed Sichuan Province.
At that time, the core module Tianhe had several sections, including those for working, sleeping, dining and exercising. The videos of Shenzhou-13 crew practicing calligraphy and playing Taichi became social media hits.
China completed the construction of its space station in 2022, with one core module and two lab modules forming a 110-square-meter orbital structure. Oxygen can be fully regenerated, and water recovery exceeds 95 percent.
Since then, long-duration spaceflights have become routine, and the Chinese "space home" can host up to six astronauts in orbit at a time.
Space residency is also set to last even longer. One member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, currently aboard the Tiangong, will conduct a one-year in-orbit stay. Moreover, as China pushes further into deep-space exploration, these extended stays will become the norm, which means astronauts' diets will be more important than ever.

item.title: Asian Games | Day 14 roundup: China achieves best result at overseas Asiad, Wong wins historic tennis gold
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
China members celebrate after taking the men's football bronze medal at the 2026 Asian Games in Toyota, Aichi Prefecture, Japan, Oct. 3, 2026. (Xinhua/Lui Siu Wai)
NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- China reached 169 gold medals at the 2026 Asian Games after Saturday's penultimate day of competition, surpassing its previous record for the most golds won at an overseas edition of the Games.
China won both the men's and women's golf team titles, with the men's victory delivering the delegation's 166th gold and breaking the previous overseas record of 165 set at the 2006 Games in Doha.
Li Wenqi added another gold in women's windsurfing, while Guo Pu won the B-Girls breaking title. Defending champion Liu Qingyi took bronze.
China also won the group all-around title as rhythmic gymnastics made its Asian Games debut, finishing ahead of host Japan and bronze medalist Kazakhstan.
Uzbekistan's Takhmina Ikromova successfully defended her individual all-around title, with China's Wang Qi and Wang Zilu taking silver and bronze, respectively.
"I'm happy that I was able to perform all four of my routines well today. I still had some small mistakes, but I'm happy I made it to the end and that it was enough for my second Asian Games gold," Ikromova said.
Coleman Wong (L) greets Wu Yibing after their men's singles tennis final at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Oct. 3, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Zeguo)
In tennis, Coleman Wong became the first player from Hong Kong, China to win an Asian Games gold medal in the sport, beating China's Wu Yibing 6-2, 6-4 in the men's singles final. The victory also secured Wong a place at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Wong broke Wu twice to take control of the opening set. The second remained level at 4-4 before Wong broke serve in the ninth game and served out the match.
"Before the Games started, I was just hoping to win a medal, regardless of the color. But honestly, now reaching this point, winning this medal, you can call it unlocking an achievement," said Wong, 22.
Wu took his second Asian Games silver medal, having also finished runner-up at Jakarta in 2018.
On the football pitch, South Korea edged Japan 1-0 in the men's final, while China ended a 28-year wait for an Asian Games men's football medal by beating Uzbekistan 4-3 on penalties in the bronze-medal match after a 2-2 draw.
It was also China's first medal in the event since the Asian Games men's football tournament adopted an under-23 format in 2002.
China goalkeeper Li Hao saved two penalties in the shootout before Peng Xiao converted the decisive spot kick.
China's Shan Changshun (C) in action during the men's rugby sevens gold medal match against Hong Kong, China at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Oct. 3, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Haobo)
China took silver in both rugby sevens events. The men's team achieved its best Asian Games finish despite losing 26-0 to Hong Kong, China in the final, while the women's team fell to Japan.
Japan continued its dominance of women's softball with a 7-0 victory over China to claim its seventh consecutive Asian Games title.
In beach volleyball, Qatar's Cherif Samba and Ahmed Janko came from behind to beat their Indonesian opponents 2-1 and secure a third successive Asian Games men's title.
China took silver in the women's 57kg and over-67kg taekwondo events, finishing its campaign in the sport with one gold and two silvers.
China's Li Lei (R) spikes the ball during the men's volleyball bronze medal match against Pakistan at the 2026 Asian Games in Okazaki, Aichi Prefecture, Japan, Oct. 3, 2026. (Xinhua/Jia Yuchen)
China missed out on a medal in men's volleyball after losing 3-0 to Pakistan in the bronze-medal match. Pakistan claimed its first Asian Games medal in the event in 64 years, while Iran beat Japan 3-1 in the final to secure a fourth consecutive title.
The International Testing Agency also reported two more doping cases Saturday. India's kurash athlete Yash Kumar Chauhan and Uzbekistan rugby player Umar Usmonov have been provisionally suspended after testing positive for banned substances.
The final two equestrian gold medals will be decided Sunday.
China leads the medal table with 169 golds, 89 silvers and 83 bronzes. Japan is second with 83 golds, 95 silvers and 91 bronzes, followed by South Korea with 39 golds, 43 silvers and 68 bronzes.

item.title: Why the World Places Greater Trust in China?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-01
In this golden autumn, as heartfelt greetings of "Happy Birthday, China!" echo across continents and oceans, why does the world steadfastly choose China?
This profound trust is sparked by the spontaneous ease of "China Travel," anchored by resilient supply chains that steady the global economy, and cemented by China's commitment as a responsible major country to mutual respect and solidarity through thick and thin.
Listen to these genuine voices from around the world, and discover the true depth of this cross-continental trust!

item.title: Flag-raising ceremony held at Tian'anmen Square to celebrate 77th founding anniversary of PRC
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-01
A flag-raising ceremony to celebrate the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China (PRC) was held at Tian'anmen Square in Beijing on Thursday.
The Guard of Honor of the Chinese People's Liberation Army escorted the national flag to the square, while the military band played the national anthem.
Many people from across China gathered at the square to watch the ceremony.

item.title: Activities held across China to celebrate National Day
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-01
Cities across China are decorating landmark sites with national flags and floral displays as National Day arrives, and people hold various activities to celebrate the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China.
